Fresh floods and landslides set off by heavy rain and storms have killed at least 14 people in Nepal and left another 11 missing, with authorities warning on Sunday that more flash floods were possible. The warnings covered 49 of Nepal's 77 districts, more than half of which faced a high risk of flooding, as water levels in major rivers kept rising. The video filmed at 5:30pm, local time, on Sunday, September 27 shows the latest destruction. This isn't a scene from a film. This is a heartbreaking reality that still exists in parts of Nepal. For some women and girls, getting their period means being sent away from their own home to spend the night in a small shed, away from their families. They are left to face cold nights, fear, loneliness, and the danger of snakes, insects, and wild animals—all because of a natural biological process. Menstruation should never be a reason for exclusion or shame. Take a moment and ask yourself: If it were someone you love—your daughter, your sister, your wife, or your mother—would you accept this as "tradition"? Some customs deserve to be questioned, especially when they put lives and dignity at risk. Every woman deserves to feel safe, respected, and valued, no matter what day of the month it is. Let's raise awareness, start conversations, and stand together to end harmful practices like this. In the remote, almost otherworldly Mustang region of Nepal, roughly 10,000 caves are carved into towering, crumbling cliffs — and some of their openings sit more than 100 feet above the valley floor, with no stairs, no path, and no visible way in. 🕳️👁️ Today, even trained researchers can only reach them by dangling from ropes. The caves have been used for thousands of years, in waves: as early as 1000 BC, people sealed their dead inside them; much later, families turned some into cliffside homes; and Buddhist monks carved others into silent chambers for meditation. Then in 2007, a local shepherd led explorers to a hidden cave covered in 55 ancient painted scenes — and another chamber, perched 700 feet up, held more than 8,000 handwritten pages. The strangest part? Erosion has long since stripped away the ledges and paths that once led up to them, leaving the entrances stranded in sheer rock. And to this day, no record says who dug the very first cave — or why they climbed so impossibly high. How do you carve a city into a cliff with no way up? 👇 #AI #mystery #didyouknow #unexplained #nepal
